issues.body:
## What Quentin saw (2026-09-16)

On the board, PR #114 appears three times: its own card, and the two issues it closes (#100, #117) each tagged « PR #114 », all in « In review ». None of the three says whether the PR has been reviewed, by whom, how many passes, or what the last verdict was. That information exists only in the PR body (sections `## Review pass N (Reviewer C, date)`), written by hand after each pass.

## Expected

The PR card carries the review state, derived from facts, never typed:

- reviewer and date of the last pass,
- pass number (the loop has a budget of four),
- last verdict: `approve` / `request_changes`, with the count of major and minor findings,
- « approved, waiting for merge » when the last pass has no major.

The issue cards closed by that PR inherit the same state next to their « PR #N » tag, so the three cards agree.

## Where the facts are

- Today: the `## Review pass` sections of the PR body (a stable format could be parsed, like `## Verified` is).
- Better: the `review_verdict` tool calls in Nodal (`tool_calls`, verdict + findings), once #124 makes the verdict the deliverable of a review job — the portal would then read the same source as the parent job.

## Not in scope

Running reviews from the portal. The board only reports.
issues.title: The board says a PR is 'in review' but never says where the review stands: pass count, verdict, reviewer

issues.body:
## What was observed (2026-09-16, six reviews run through Alfred → Reviewer C)

Reviewer C ends every review with the `review_verdict` tool (verdict, summary, findings). That call is recorded in `tool_calls`, but the job's `result` — what the parent receives through the delegation contract — is the model's last sentence, e.g. « J'ai couvert toutes les questions. Je constate maintenant le verdict et je livre les constats. » (job `ebf1951a`, PR #113, 428 characters, while the verdict carried 5 findings).

Consequences seen in the database:
- Alfred, receiving a sentence instead of a report, **delegated a second review of the same PR** on its own (PR #113: child `ebf1951a` completed, then a new child under the same parent `417a3db5`; PR #120: same pattern under `b46e0410`). Each duplicate costs 30 to 40 minutes of glm-5.3-flash.
- The person driving the reviews has to read `tool_calls` by hand to find the verdict.

## Expected

The verdict recorded by `review_verdict` IS the deliverable of a review job. It must travel through the typed delegation record (the carrier #108 chose), so that the parent receives verdict + findings and never re-delegates a job that already produced one. The parent's own final answer then carries the report verbatim.

## Where to look

- `packages/tools/src/builtin/review-verdict.ts` — the tool only presents a card.
- `apps/runner/src/job/*` — how a child's terminal result is built and delivered to the parent (#108).
- `packages/orchestration` — the delegation contract and the "no deliverable" detection.
issues.title: A review_verdict recorded by a sub-agent never reaches its parent: the child answers with a sentence, and the parent delegates again

issues.body:
## What happened

On the night of 2026-09-15 (02:13 local), Alfred called its `attach_agent` tool on `reviewer-c` while running a review job. Reviewer C was already a worker of Lead-Dev. The result is one agent shown under two orchestrators on the Agents page. A one-shot script then created a new `reviewer` agent and inserted it under both Alfred and Lead-Dev at once.

Quentin's decision (2026-09-16): **one agent, one place.** An agent never appears in two teams.

## Where the product currently allows it

- `agent_assignments` is many-to-many with a UNIQUE on (orchestrator_id, sub_agent_id) only — nothing forbids a second orchestrator for the same sub-agent.
- `apps/web/src/app/(dashboard)/agents/AddWorkerModal.tsx` is documented as *purely additive*: it calls `moveWorkerAssignmentAction` with `fromOrchestratorId: null`, so a worker keeps its previous team.
- `packages/tools/src/builtin/meta-ops/attach-agent.ts` (`attachAgentToOrchestrator` in `packages/db/src/repos/agents.ts`) inserts a new row without checking whether the agent already has a parent.
- `createAgentRepo` accepts `subAgentIds` / `assignToOrchestratorId` without the same check.

## What must change

1. **Database**: a UNIQUE constraint on `agent_assignments.sub_agent_id` (migration + journal + inline test SQL, per CLAUDE.md), after a one-time cleanup of existing duplicates.
2. **Web**: adding a worker to a team MOVES it (the modal passes the current parent as `fromOrchestratorId`), and the UI says so.
3. **Tools**: `attach_agent` on an agent that already has a parent fails loud, naming the current parent (invariant #4). It never re-parents silently.
4. Tests that fail first for each path, verified by mutation.

## Not in scope

Whether an orchestrator may use a worker from another team through delegation without owning it — separate decision.
issues.title: An agent belongs to exactly one team: the UI, the attach_agent tool and the database must all refuse a second parent

issues.body:
Reviewer A (qwen/qwen3.8-max, OpenRouter) worked 12 turns over 16 minutes on a read-only code review (20 file reads), then turn 13 hit `LLMTimeoutError: LLM call timed out after 300000ms`. The job went `failed`, `result` = "⚠️ The task could not be completed (LLM call timed out after 300000ms: openrouter/qwen/qwen3.8-max) and no explanation was provided." Twelve turns of reading were thrown away; nothing partial reached the parent (Alfred reported the reviewer as blocked, which is correct behaviour on his side).

Two defects:
1. **A single timed-out turn kills a job that had been progressing.** Stale-retry exists for timeouts (`packages/llm` withStaleRetry), so either it did not apply on this path, or its budget was exhausted by one 5-minute call. After a late timeout the runner should retry the turn once with the same messages (the transcript is intact), and only then fail; failing must keep the transcript as the deliverable-so-far for the parent (typed record, `exit_reason: timeout`).
2. **The user-facing text is the raw error string.** Same as #119: the runner has the facts (provider, model, turn, elapsed) and should say them, not paste the exception.

## Verified
```
$ node q.mjs "select a.name, c.status, length(c.result), left(c.error,80) from agent_jobs c join agents a on a.id=c.agent_id where c.parent_job_id='31d9e0cb-4626-453b-97b0-458bfc9621bb'"
Reviewer A · failed · 132 · LLM call timed out after 300000ms: openrouter/qwen/qwen3.8-max
Reviewer C · completed · 12509
$ node q.mjs "select turn, model_effective, error from llm_calls where job_id=<Reviewer A child> order by created_at"
turns 1-12: qwen/qwen3.8-max-0902, no error · turn 13: LLMTimeoutError after 300000ms
$ node q.mjs "select tool_name, count(*) from tool_calls where job_id=<Reviewer A child>"  → file_read etc. (12 turns of real work)
```
Parent job 31d9e0cb-4626-453b-97b0-458bfc9621bb, 2026-09-16 01:22 → 01:38 local. Reviewer A's model was switched from gemini-3.7-flash to qwen3.8-max at 01:15 (agents.updated_at), after #119.
issues.title: One LLM timeout at turn 13 discards 12 turns of work: the job fails with nothing, and the user gets the raw error

issues.body:
Reviewer A (`google/gemini-3.7-flash` through OpenRouter, provider Google AI Studio) cannot run a single turn: the first LLM call fails with `400 Request contains an invalid argument` and the job ends `failed` at turn 1 with no tool used. The same instruction on Reviewer C (`z-ai/glm-5.3-flash`) runs.

The result delivered to the user is the raw provider JSON followed by "and no explanation was provided". That is fail-loud, but unreadable: nothing tells the user that the model rejected the request shape, nor what to change (another model, fewer tools).

Likely cause to verify first: the tool schema sent to Gemini (43 tools on this agent). Gemini's function-calling is stricter than OpenAI-compatible providers on JSON Schema keywords (`additionalProperties`, `$schema`, `anyOf`, empty `properties`) — the memory of the Gemini provider fix of 2026-07-12 says the same class of problem was fixed at the native provider level; the OpenRouter route may not go through it.

## Verified
```
$ node q.mjs "select status, turn, tools_used, total_cost_usd from agent_jobs where id='452b8aa3-07bf-4c71-ac33-40d35d3389e5'"
status: failed · turn: 1 · tools_used: [] · total_cost_usd: 0
$ node q.mjs "select model_effective, provider, array_length(tool_names,1), left(error,80) from llm_calls where job_id='452b8aa3-…'"
google/gemini-3.7-flash · openrouter · 43 · AI_APICallError: [Google AI Studio] Request contains an invalid argument.
```
Job 452b8aa3-07bf-4c71-ac33-40d35d3389e5, 2026-09-16 00:56 local, entity 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000002.

## Expected
1. A job on a Gemini model through OpenRouter runs its first turn (test: the tool schema we emit is accepted by Gemini; a fixture with the 43 real tools, replayed against the provider's schema validator or recorded response).
2. When a provider rejects the request at turn 1, the user-facing reason names the provider, the status, and the one actionable hint the runner can give (try another model for this agent), instead of dumping the JSON.
issues.title: Gemini via OpenRouter rejects every job with 43 tools: 400 INVALID_ARGUMENT at turn 1, and the user gets a raw JSON dump

issues.body:
Four residues from the Codex review of #108, kept out of that PR on purpose. They share one root: the delegation outcome travels as a typed record between a parent and its own child, and as free TEXT everywhere else.

## 1. A grandchild's failure does not reach the grandparent

A parent whose child delegated further sees only the child's result. The line the harness appends (`[delegation stopped: assign_x — no deliverable]`) is part of that text, and #108 briefly read it back to re-raise the failure one level up. That was removed before merge: a child is a model, so it can write that line itself, with any name in it, and the harness would then deliver an invented failure as a fact. The review measured it.

**What a fix has to carry.** `DelegationOutcomeRecord` (`packages/orchestration/src/router/resume.ts`) is the typed object a parent receives for its own child: `{status, summary, error, exit_reason, tools_used}`. The record needs a field for the failures the child itself could not resolve — filled by the harness from its own bookkeeping, never parsed out of prose — and `resumeDelegated` has to merge it into the parent's set. Then the notice, the propagation and the delivery all read the same authenticated source.

## 2. A propagated failure survives a real repair

Once a name is in the failed set, only a later delivery from that same specialist clears it. If the repair went through a different route — the parent redid the work, or a second specialist covered it — the line stays on a result that is now complete. It is a stale statement rather than a false one, but it is a statement to the user, so it counts.

Same root: with the typed record, the sub-tree's outcome would be known rather than inferred from a name.

## 3. `failJob` paths are not atomic with their delivery intent

#108 wired the T08 seam (`finalizeJobSuccess`'s `prepareDelivery`) so the outbox row is written INSIDE the terminal transaction on the success path. The failure paths have no such seam: `failJob` writes the terminal row, then the harness notice is prepared afterwards. A crash in between leaves a finished job with nothing to deliver, and no drain can recover it.

**Where.** `apps/runner/src/job/execute.ts` — the `telegram_not_delivered` paths (text branch and `return_result` branch) and the `return_result{status:'blocked'}` finalization; `apps/runner/src/job/finalize.ts` for the shape to mirror.

## 4. The success path's atomicity is not covered by a test

The wiring is there; no test exercises it, because a tool-only channel cannot complete in the delegation fixture — the send tool is not in the seeded agent's whitelist, so the job always ends on the failure path. Either the fixture gains a working send adapter, or the seam is tested directly in `finalize.test.ts` with a `delivery` + `prepareDelivery` pair.

## Scope

Found by the Codex review of #108 (control pass and targeted pass on the harness delivery). #108 closes #107 and #115; these four are the part that needs a different carrier, not a bigger patch.
issues.title: The delegation outcome travels as text where it should travel typed

issues.body:
`nodal-agents` proves a write for file targets only. A **directory** target — the `cwd` of a shell command, or the whole write scope of a harness turn — stays **declarative**: `observedDeliverableKeys` adds its key on the strength of the target alone, with nothing read from the disk.

Consequence: a `run_command` that succeeds **without writing anything**, with its `cwd` on a project, still gets `produced = true` on that project, and `declare_verification` then grants it the right to say how that project is verified. This is exactly the hole that #60 closed for file targets, left open for the shell surface.

It is named in the code (`packages/tools/src/verification/observed.ts`, header and the `dirTargets` loop) and was deliberately left out of PR #75's scope. Raised again by the Codex post-merge review of #75 (finding 4), which is why it is written down here rather than only in a comment.

**Where**

- `packages/tools/src/verification/observed.ts` — `observedDeliverableKeys`, the `for (const p of projects(rebasedDirs)) keys.add(p.key)` loop.
- `packages/tools/src/execute.ts` — the call site that passes `dirTargets`.

**What a fix would have to decide**

Constating what a shell wrote under a directory means a tree snapshot on each command. The cost is the whole question: a full walk is out of the question on a large repository, and any cheap approximation (mtime of the folder, a depth cap, an ignore list) is a new hole that has to be named rather than assumed. The checkpoint snapshot taken once per turn does not answer it either — it excludes `dist/` and is taken too early.

An honest smaller step: stop crediting `produced` on a directory target alone, and say in the tool's own output that nothing was constated. That turns a false green into a visible absence, which is the side that costs the least.

**Why `debt` and not a bug**

Nothing regressed. This is the part of "a write is constated on disk" that was never delivered, and the current comment says so. The issue exists so that the limit is findable outside the file that carries it.
issues.title: Directory targets are still credited as writes without anything being constated

issues.body:
Found by the Codex review of the #66 debt (PR #99), passes 2 and 4, and acknowledged there as out of that PR's scope. It predates #66.

## 1. A code project's epoch does not cover an intent posted before the proof

`finalize.ts` decides a proof is stale by comparing `epoch` and `manifestHash` across the two transactions. For a code project the epoch is the shared one in `code_projects`, bumped by another job's mutation intent. That ordering is permitted by the code:

1. B posts its intent and bumps the epoch to 8 — `packages/tools/src/verification/intent.ts:465`
2. B waits for its checkpoint; the WRITE happens after — `packages/tools/src/execute.ts:636`, `:662`
3. A captures epoch 8, then proves the OLD content
4. B writes invalid content
5. A re-reads epoch 8 and the same manifest: **stale green**

A's own dirty generation never changes, because the write was not A's.

The document verifier closed its half of this in #99 by reporting what the proof actually READ (`ProofResult.provedManifestHash`) and having finalize compare against that. A code project has no equivalent: its proof runs commands, and nothing summarises the tree it ran against. Options worth weighing:

- have the code-project verifier report a digest of the tree it proved (expensive, and "the tree" is not well defined once `dist/` and friends are excluded);
- bump the epoch at the WRITE rather than at the intent — but the intent exists precisely to mark the project dirty BEFORE the write, so this would trade one hole for another;
- keep the epoch where it is and add a second, cheap witness taken immediately before and after the proof.

## 2. Two derivations of a project's identity, still separate

Pass 2 of the same review, findings R4 and R5:

- `packages/tools/src/verification/intent.ts:176` resolves project roots with `hasMarker` alone.
- `packages/tools/src/lib/code-projects.ts:198` (the Code screen) derives its own.

#99 made a DECLARED project count as a project root for the intent and the observation seam, so those two agree. The Code screen was not part of that change and still derives separately, so a project declared without a manifest can be named differently in the two places.

## Why it matters

Both are the same shape as the defects #99 fixed: a guard that looks like it covers a case and does not. The first one records a green verdict on content nobody verified — the exact class of bug the whole "Vérifier & Corriger" plan exists to prevent.

## Before touching this

Read `docs/validation/rapport-review-pr66-passe*.md` on PR #99. Four passes sit behind the current document rules, and several earlier shapes were wrong in ways that are not obvious from the code.
issues.title: The verification primitive's staleness guards do not cover a write whose intent precedes the proof

tour 1  14:19:15  35 k jetons  cache 0        $0,0399
tour 2  14:52:57  35 k jetons  cache 0        $0,0396   ← 33 min après

issues.body:
`pg_ctl stop -m fast` does not return on the Linux CI runner once the postmaster has been through crash recovery.

## The measurement

`apps/cli/src/tests/postgres-logging.pg.test.ts` starts a real embedded cluster in a temp directory on a free port. Its third case, `records the pid of a backend killed from outside, and how it died`, kills one backend with SIGKILL — which is the 2026-09-15 incident reproduced, and which the postmaster answers by restarting every other backend (`restart_after_crash = on`).

The teardown then calls `handle.stop()`, i.e. the package's `pg_ctl stop -m fast`. On GitHub's `ubuntu-latest` runner it does not come back:

| Run | What the teardown did |
|---|---|
| 35054484082 (twice, including a `--failed` re-run) | `Error: Hook timed out in 120000ms`, all three cases green |
| 35056898578 | `pg_ctl stop did not return within 60s (waited 60002ms)` |

The three cases pass in 36ms, 4ms and 1ms. Only the stop hangs. On a real Windows machine the same file runs green end to end in 5s, stop included.

## What was done, and what was not

`test(cli): the cluster teardown says what it could not stop` (PR #114) gave the stop a 60s budget of its own and made it SAY what it could not clean, instead of the hook dying anonymously at 120s with no word about which of its two lines hung. The temp directory is removed either way.

That is a diagnosis, not a fix. The suite now reports on its cases rather than on its cleanup, and on that runner it leaves a postmaster running against a temp data directory until the runner is discarded. On a developer's machine the printed line names that directory.

## What to find out

- Whether the postmaster is still in crash recovery when the stop arrives, in which case `-m fast` is waiting for a recovery it cannot interrupt, and the test should wait for the cluster to settle before stopping it.
- Whether the logging collector is what holds the process open: `logging_collector = on` (issue #111) makes the collector own the postmaster's stderr, which is already why `embedded-postgres`'s own `start()` promise never settles. A stop that waits on that stream would never return either.
- Whether `-m immediate` is the honest mode for a teardown that is about to delete the data directory anyway.

The first two are testable on the Linux runner from the log the cluster now keeps.
issues.title: pg_ctl stop hangs on the Linux runner after a crash-recovered cluster

issues.body:
Follow-up of PR #103 (Reviewer C, pass 1, 2026-09-16). Quentin's decision: not fixed in #103, tracked here.

## The gap

`packages/tools/src/projects/attach.ts` chooses the job's project with `firstMatch(targets, byDepth(projects))`: the deepest REGISTERED project of the entity containing the written file wins. The mutation intent (`resolveProjectRoots`) reasons on the workspace roots instead. The two agree as long as nested registered projects derive from the same workspace roots.

## When they diverge

`app` is attached and declared; `app/src` and `app/src/lib` are already in the registry (attached by another agent of the same entity, or declared before the fix of #103 that stopped declaring subfolders of a declared project). Target `app/src/lib/mod.ts`: the intent marks `app`; attach picks `app/src/lib`. The job is filed under a child of the project the intent names, and `declare_verification` for `app` can refuse work that was really done.

## Not observed in any real workspace so far; needs pre-existing nested rows.

## Expected

One rule for both: attach follows `resolveProjectRoots` (the intent's rule) when choosing among registered projects; a registered descendant of the intended root is not preferred over it. Test that fails first on the three-level case (`app`, `app/src`, `app/src/lib`), fix verified by mutation.
issues.title: attach() picks the deepest registered project containing the target, not the project the intent names

## Observed, 2026-09-15 21:05 local

`~/.nodalai/logs/pnpm-dev.log`: someone ran `pnpm dev` (turbo) in `D:\APPS\NodalAI` while Quentin's stack was healthy on :3000 / :3001 / :25444 (runner 200, web 307 at 21:00). The `nodal-agents:dev` task is `tsx src/index.ts` = `up`. Its pre-flight found the three live processes on the configured ports, printed `Cleaning up before starting…`, and killed them (`apps/cli/src/commands/up.ts:344-360`: every process found on our ports or owning our data dir goes into `orphans[]`, and `orphans.length > 0` means kill). The turbo run then failed on `@nodal-agents/web#dev` (exit 1), so nothing replaced what it had killed. The stack stayed down until 23:29, when it was noticed and relaunched by hand.

This is the third time today the stack went down under an agent's feet (#111 records the two `57P02` crashes), and the first with a log that names the mechanism.

## The defect

`up` has no notion of "a healthy stack is ALREADY running here". An orphan is a process that survived a dead launcher; a process answering `/api/health` with `{"ok":true,"db":"ok"}` on the configured port, with a valid `postmaster.pid` for our data dir, is not an orphan, it is the product, running. Killing it is the same class as #97 and #100: a pid is treated as a nuisance because of where it was found, not because of what it is.

## Expected

Before any cleanup, `up` probes the configured runner and web ports and the data dir's lockfile. If the runner answers healthy AND the lockfile names a live postmaster for our data dir, `up` refuses with `Nodal-Agents is already running (runner pid N, web pid M, postgres pid P) — use \`nodal-agents down\` first`, exit 1, nothing killed. Only when the health probe fails does the orphan pre-flight run. Mutation to prove it: remove the refusal, the test that starts a fake healthy runner on the port must go red.

This belongs with PR #114 (Postgres logs, no unproven kill): same file, same rule, same agent.

issues.body:
On a tool-only channel (Telegram, Discord, Slack), a job that ends in failure after its redelivery nudges are exhausted stores its reason in `agent_jobs.result` and sends nothing. The user is left with silence.

**Where**

`apps/runner/src/job/execute.ts` — the `telegram_not_delivered` paths, and the `return_result{status:'blocked'}` finalization just above them. Once `redeliveryNudges` reaches `MAX_REDELIVERY_NUDGES`, the code goes straight to `failJob`. `failJob` writes a user-facing reason into the row; no delivery is prepared, and that branch drains none.

**Why it matters**

`status='blocked'` is the honest exit the runner offers an agent that cannot finish: it exists so the user is told WHY instead of being left waiting. On a channel where only a tool reaches the user, that promise is not kept — the explanation exists in the database and nowhere the user can see it.

It is worse in the case that motivated #107: a delegation failed, the parent says so honestly, its sends fail, and the user gets exactly what the incident produced — nothing.

**What a fix has to decide**

The runner already has a delivery primitive that does not depend on the model (`prepared` deliveries, drained by `drainDeliveries`). The question is whether a harness-authored delivery is acceptable here, and in whose voice: invariant #2 forbids user-facing text written by the runner in the agent's name. A platform-marked line — the same shape as the existing `[livraison effectuée : …]` metadata — is probably the answer, but it is a product call, not a mechanical one.

**Scope**

Found by the Codex review of #108 (fourth pass, finding 2), where it is out of scope: this path predates that branch and applies to every failed job on a tool-only channel, not only a delegated one.
issues.title: A blocked job on a tool-only channel keeps its reason in the database

issues.body:
Twice on 2026-09-15 (during the delegation bench of PR #108, and once more around 18:50 local) the runner logged `57P02: terminating connection because of crash of another server process` (`~/.nodalai/logs/runner.log` ~L64356 onward). The postmaster restarted its backends, the runner lost every connection, the launcher watchdog printed DEGRADED, then a child process exited and the launcher shut the whole stack down ("Stopped. Goodbye!", `%TEMP%\nodal-dev.log`). Quentin's stack was down twice without anyone stopping it.

What cannot be established: WHICH backend died and WHY. The embedded Postgres runs with stderr logging and no `logging_collector`; `~/.nodalai/pg-data` has no `log/` directory and `~/.nodalai/logs/` has no postgres log. The only trace is the runner's side of the disconnect.

Two things to do:

1. Capture Postgres logs: `logging_collector = on`, `log_directory` under `~/.nodalai/logs/`, rotation, and `log_min_messages = warning` at least. A crash must leave the signal number and the pid of the backend that died.
2. Once the log exists, attribute the crash. The prime suspect is a kill by pid of a Postgres backend belonging to the live cluster: `down.ts`, `sweepRecordedChildren` and `taskkill /T` kill recorded pids without consulting ownership (issue #100), and two `up`/`down` cycles from a worktree happened on this machine during the same window. A backend killed from outside is exactly what "crash of another server process" looks like from the inside.

Also worth deciding: should the launcher shut down the whole stack when ONE child exits after a Postgres hiccup, or restart the child? Today the answer is "shut down, fail loud" (invariant #4), which is correct, but the failure is loud only in a terminal nobody is watching when the stack runs detached.
issues.title: Embedded Postgres leaves no log: a backend crash (57P02, twice on 2026-09-15) cannot be attributed

Its scenario B is worse than absent: it asserts "at least 1 child job was created" (`agent-flows.spec.ts:169-173`) — a count, not a result (invariant #5). Issue #107 would have passed it green: a child job existed, it just delivered nothing.

Two ways out, pick one per journey:

1. delete the journeys that only a real model can exercise, and say so — a spec nobody runs is a claim of coverage that does not exist;
2. rewrite them without a model, the way `delegation-outcome.spec.ts` (PR #108) does: seed the rows, drive the screen, assert what the user sees.

Whichever is chosen, `requireLmStudio` should go with the last caller: a helper that can only pass on one developer's machine invites the next dead spec.

No text, no delivery tool (it has none: an internal job carries no `telegram_send_message`). The runner acknowledged and finalized the child with `result = NULL`.

`compileChildResults` (apps/runner/src/job/state.ts:175) then handed the parent `## Researcher\n(no output)`. Alfred's next turn sent "Recherche lancée sur la longueur de Planck, je te renvoie la synthèse dès que c'est prêt" (40 output tokens), then `return_result success` (12 tokens). The user received a promise for a result that had already failed to exist. Nothing else ever arrived.

## Two defects, both runner-side (invariant #4: no silent smart fallbacks)

1. **An internal (delegated) job that signals `success` while `agent_jobs.result` is empty and no text was produced is finalized as completed.** The delivery guard only covers `TOOL_ONLY_DELIVERY_CHANNELS` (telegram/discord/slack), on the premise that "internal exposes result directly, so a text-only completion is fine" (execute.ts:299). Text-only, yes. Text-less, no. The runner must refuse the signal and nudge once: "you signalled success but produced nothing: write the deliverable as your reply text, then signal again", and if the second attempt is still empty, finalize as **failed** with that reason, never as completed.

2. **The parent receives "(no output)" as ordinary child output.** It should be an explicit outcome: the tool-result of `assign_<slug>` must say the delegation produced nothing (status failed + reason), so the orchestrator's options are to redo, re-delegate, or tell the user; today the text "(no output)" is indistinguishable from a specialist that answered "(no output)".

## Not a defect here

- The "Mets en ligne sur cloudflare" line the user saw in the transcript is Telegram thread history replayed into the job (an earlier message of the same chat). Nothing about Cloudflare was executed on this job.
- The Researcher has the `obsidian` skill assigned and `research-scope-discipline` told it to search the vault first; it read the latter and skipped the former. One observation on one model; skills are guidance, not switches.

## Proof expected

Test on execute.ts: an internal job whose final assistant turn is `return_result success` with no text and no delivery tool call must NOT reach `completed` with an empty result (first a nudge, then `failed`). Mutation: remove the guard, the test goes red. A second test on the parent side: the assign tool-result for a failed child carries the failure, not "(no output)".
issues.title: A delegated job can signal success with nothing produced, and the parent then tells the user the work is "launched"

issues.body:
Carried out of the Codex review of #98 (pass 5, finding R3; restated in passes 6-10 and each time acknowledged as out of that PR's scope). It predates #98 and is not caused by it.

## What #98 fixed, and where it stops

#98 rebuilt how `up` decides that a Postgres process is OURS: the data directory answers (`postmaster.pid` is written BY the postmaster that holds it), the process table only confirms, and nothing is killed that a fresh reading has not confirmed. That work covers **the postgres path only**.

Everything else still kills on the faith of a recorded pid.

## The paths

**1. `up`'s non-postgres loop — `apps/cli/src/commands/up.ts:461`**

```ts
await execa('taskkill', ['/T', '/F', '/PID', String(o.pid)], { reject: false });
```

- `name` in that list identifies the CONFIGURED PORT, not the executable. A pid recorded as our runner or web, recycled onto a foreign Postgres now listening on that port, is accepted by `ourPids` and force-killed without ever passing through `ownedPgPids`.
- `/T` kills the whole tree without asking what is in it. A service in that tree can have started a Postgres against a different data directory.
- The `strangers` refusal does not protect these: they were already classified as ours before it runs.

**2. `sweepRecordedChildren` — `apps/cli/src/commands/up.ts:207`, `down.ts:138`**

It compares recorded dates, which is better than nothing, but it consults no data-dir ownership. Same shape of exposure.

**3. `down` — `apps/cli/src/commands/down.ts:56`, `:100-101`**

```ts
const pgPid = readPostmasterPid(PG_DATA_DIR);
```

It takes the pid off the lockfile and, at `:100-101`, can recommend `Stop-Process -Id <pid> -Force` or `kill -9 <pid>` against it. `readPostmasterPid` now checks line 2 (the recorded data directory), but NOT the start time, and `down` performs none of the confirmation `up` gained: a recycled pid can be recommended to the user as "our Postgres".

## Why it matters

This is the same class of defect as #97, which cost a live database on 2026-09-14: a pid is treated as an identity. A pid is not an identity — it is a number the OS reuses.

## What the fix probably looks like

`up` and `down` should share the confirmation `apps/cli/src/lib/postgres.ts` now provides, rather than each deciding on its own:

- a pid recommended or killed as Postgres goes through `postgresProcessesForDataDir` / `ownedPostgresPids`;
- `killProcessTree` / `taskkill /T` refuses, or at least reports, a tree member that is a postgres process belonging to a data directory that is not ours;
- `down` stops recommending a hard kill on a pid it has not confirmed, and says what it could not confirm instead.

## Not in scope here

The postgres ownership rule itself — that is #98, which is where the reasoning and the tests live. Read `docs/validation/rapport-review-pr98-passe*.md` before touching this: ten passes of review sit behind the current rule, and several earlier shapes of it were wrong in ways that are not obvious.
issues.title: Recorded pids are killed without consulting data-dir ownership (up's non-postgres loop, taskkill /T, sweepRecordedChildren, down)

issues.body:
## What happened

Starting a second, isolated Nodal-Agents stack killed the Postgres of the **main** install. The dashboard on `:3000` then answered:

```
{"ok":false,"db":"error","service":"nodalai-web"}
```

The web process was still alive; only its database was gone. Recovered with `down` + `up --dev` — nothing was lost, the data dir was untouched — but nothing warned, and `up` reported the kill as routine cleanup.

## Reproduction

Two installs sharing one `node_modules` (a git worktree with `node_modules` junctioned to the main checkout — the supported way to review a branch on Windows without a second `pnpm install`):

- main install: `HOME=C:\Users\kwint`, data dir `C:/Users/kwint/.nodalai/pg-data`, **Postgres on :25444**, postmaster **pid 41956**
- isolated install: scratch `USERPROFILE`, data dir `<scratch>/.nodalai/pg-data`, **Postgres on :25450**

Command run for the isolated stack:

```
set USERPROFILE=<scratch>
set HOME=<scratch>
npx tsx apps/cli/src/index.ts up --dev
```

Output:

```
Found 13 orphan processes on configured ports:
  - postgres on :25450 (pid 41956)
  - postgres on :25450 (pid 8932)
  ... (11 more)
Cleaning up before starting…
Orphans cleaned up.
```

**Pid 41956 was the main install's postmaster, listening on :25444.** It was never on :25450. It was killed.

## Two defects, one line apart

### 1. A pid is attributed to a port it was never observed on

`apps/cli/src/commands/up.ts` — the third probe pushes every returned pid with the CONFIGURED port stapled to it:

```ts
for (const pid of await postgresPidsForDataDir()) {
  orphans.push({ name: 'postgres', port: config.ports.postgres, pid });
}
```

`postgresPidsForDataDir()` reads the process table. It says nothing about ports. So `:25450` in the message is not a measurement — it is the config value, printed next to a pid that has no relationship to it. Thirteen lines all claiming the same port is the visible symptom.

### 2. The ownership test matches any install sharing the binary

`apps/cli/src/lib/postgres.ts:114`:

```ts
if (cmd.includes(dataNeedle) || cmd.includes(binNeedle)) pids.push(pid);
```

with `binNeedle = '@embedded-postgres'`. The comment above it states the rule:

> The binary path cannot be spoofed by accident: it points inside this install's node_modules, so anything running from it is ours by construction, postmaster or worker.

That is not true whenever two installs resolve to the same `node_modules` — a junctioned or symlinked worktree, or any layout where the path is shared. Both clusters' `postgres.exe` then carry the identical path, and the probe claims every one of them.

`dataNeedle` is correct and does discriminate. `binNeedle` was added on 2026-08-21 to catch `--forkchild="io_worker"` processes, which carry no data dir — a real problem, solved with a needle that is far too wide.

## What it should do

- **Never attribute a pid to a port without measuring it.** `Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort <port> -State Listen` (or the existing `pidListeningOnPort`) is the only thing that may set the `port` field. A pid found by process table alone should be reported as "postgres process for our data dir (pid N)", with no port claimed.
- **Narrow the ownership test so it cannot match a sibling install.** The binary path is shared; the data dir is not. For a worker with no data dir on its command line, tie it to a postmaster that IS ours — by parent pid (`Win32_Process.ParentProcessId`), walking up to a process whose command line carries `dataNeedle` — rather than by the binary alone.
- **Refuse rather than guess.** `up` already has exactly this rule for the web and runner ports: "Nodal-Agents will not kill a process it did not start — it could be your own work." Postgres is exempted from it, and this is what the exemption cost.

## Files

- `apps/cli/src/commands/up.ts` — the three orphan probes and the port attribution
- `apps/cli/src/lib/postgres.ts` — `postgresPidsForDataDir()`, the `binNeedle` match

issues.body:
## Ce que l'utilisateur ne peut pas faire

Il ne peut pas **lire jusqu'où va un connecteur Google avant de le connecter** — c'est-à-dire dans le seul cas où l'avertissement sert à quelque chose : la toute première fois.

La phrase « **What this connector can reach** » (« …the ENTIRE Google Drive ») est rendue par `ConnectorAddForm` (`apps/web/src/app/(dashboard)/connectors/ConnectorAddForm.tsx:36`, composant `ScopeDisclosure`). Or la carte du catalogue n'ouvre `ConnectorAddForm` que s'il existe **déjà** un identifiant compatible :

```ts
// apps/web/src/app/(dashboard)/connectors/ConnectorsMarketplaceGrid.tsx:74
const needsWizard = catalogItem.authType === 'oauth2' && compatibleCredentials.length === 0;
…
onCta={() => (needsWizard ? setWizardOpen(true) : setAddOpen(true))}
```

Sur une installation neuve, `compatibleCredentials` est vide : la carte ouvre **directement** le `CredentialWizard` (`apps/web/src/app/(dashboard)/credentials/CredentialWizard.tsx`), qui ne rend aucune divulgation de portée. L'utilisateur passe donc de « Install » à l'écran de consentement de Google sans que le produit lui ait dit, dans ses mots à lui, que le jeton atteint tout son Drive.

Une fois l'identifiant créé, la divulgation réapparaît — pour un utilisateur qui a déjà accordé l'accès. C'est l'inverse de l'intention écrite dans le fichier lui-même : « Google's own screen does say it, in Google's words, at the moment the user is already committed. This says it in ours, **while they can still walk away**. »

## La preuve

Mesure nocturne du 11/09 (`.github/workflows/qa.yml`, runner GitHub neuf, aucun connecteur configuré), rapport `apps/qa/data/playwright-run.json` :

```
apps/web/tests/e2e/connector-scope-disclosure.spec.ts:60
  « Google Drive states it reaches the ENTIRE Drive »

  expect(locator).toBeVisible() failed
  Locator: getByRole('dialog').getByText(/what this connector can reach/i)
  Expected: visible
  Timeout: 10000ms
  Error: element(s) not found
```

```
apps/web/tests/e2e/connector-scope-disclosure.spec.ts:72
  « Google Sheets and Docs disclose their reach too »

  Error: Google Sheets shows no disclosure
  expect(locator).toBeVisible() failed
  Locator: getByRole('dialog').getByText(/what this connector can reach/i)
```

Le parcours est **juste** : il ouvre le catalogue par l'onglet « Library », désigne la carte par son ancre et clique le bouton réel. C'est le produit qui ne tient pas sa promesse.

Cela **répond à #72** : ce n'est pas un écart d'environnement au sens d'un service manquant, et ce n'est pas une régression de code non plus. C'est une branche d'interface que la machine de Quentin ne prend jamais (il a un identifiant Google), et qu'un runner neuf prend toujours. Le vert local était le vert du mauvais chemin.

## Le troisième cas est vert pour une mauvaise raison

`connector-scope-disclosure.spec.ts:86` — « a connector whose reach matches its name shows NO disclosure » (Gmail) — passe sur le runner parce que **le wizard ne montre jamais rien**, pas parce que Gmail est un cas où il ne faut rien montrer. Il passera vraiment le jour où ce défaut sera corrigé.

## Piste

`ScopeDisclosure` doit vivre là où l'utilisateur arrive réellement : dans le `CredentialWizard` à l'étape « formulaire », quand le type est connu (`initialType` / `config`). Le texte est déjà dans le catalogue (`catalogItem.scopeDisclosure`, `packages/shared` — un test unitaire y garantit déjà qu'une portée large ne peut pas être sans divulgation).

## Non corrigé ici

Le lot de triage (#55) ne touche pas au produit. Les deux cas restent rouges jusqu'à ce que cette issue soit fermée — c'est voulu : ils décrivent un vrai manque.
issues.title: Connecting Google for the first time never says how far the token reaches

faut penser à ouvrir n'existe pas.

## Ce qu'on livre

**La sévérité se déduit de faits**, jamais d'un réglage à la main : est-ce
qu'une capacité du produit tombe, est-ce que c'est sur `main`, est-ce que
c'est neuf ou déjà connu par une issue ouverte.

**Une alerte, une seule pour commencer** : quelque chose passe au rouge sur
`main`, le portail **ouvre l'issue lui-même**. Elle atterrit dans le Kanban, à
sa colonne. Pas de mail, pas de canal de plus.

Dépend du registre de capacités : sans lui, le portail ne sait pas ce qui est
grave.

`apps/qa/data/history.ndjson` garde une ligne **par collecte**. Il en faut une
**par test et par exécution**. C'est ce qui permet de dire « ce test a tourné
47 fois, échoué 3 fois, toujours sous Windows » — au lieu de « instable »,
qu'on calcule aujourd'hui sur un seul run, ce qui est presque un contresens :
l'instabilité ne se voit que dans le temps.

## Ce qu'on livre

- **La collecte d'abord**, avant l'écran. Ce lot a une contrainte que les
  autres n'ont pas : il a besoin de temps. Un historique lancé dans trois
  semaines vaut trois semaines de moins. Les données s'accumulent pendant
  qu'on travaille ailleurs.
- Une fenêtre glissante, pour que le fichier ne grossisse pas sans fin.
- Puis l'écran : la tendance, l'âge d'un problème, et les tests réellement
  instables triés par nuisance.

Le seul graphe actuel montre le NOMBRE de tests. C'est une métrique de vanité.

issues.body:
« `@nodal-agents/web` à 78 % » ne dit rien à personne. La question qu'on se
pose vraiment, c'est « est-ce qu'un utilisateur peut connecter Notion ce
matin, et qu'est-ce qui le prouve ». Rien ne relie aujourd'hui un test à une
capacité du produit.

## Ce qu'on livre

Un registre nomme ce que le produit sait faire — dérivé des 33 parcours e2e
et des 32 écrans existants, pas d'une liste inventée. Chaque test déclare la
capacité qu'il prouve avec une étiquette `@cap:<slug>` dans son titre, lue
telle quelle par Vitest et par Playwright.

L'écran montre une capacité par ligne : verte, rouge, ou **jamais prouvée**.
Cette dernière colonne est la seule qui compte vraiment — c'est la liste de
ce qu'on croit livré.

## Les deux portes

- une étiquette qui ne correspond à aucune capacité du registre fait rougir
  (sinon l'étiquetage pourrit en trois semaines) ;
- une capacité **exigée** sans un seul test qui la prouve fait rougir.

L'exigence part sur une poignée de capacités et s'étend par vagues. Une porte
qui exige tout dès le premier jour se fait désactiver le deuxième.

## Précédent

`Section.tests` du banc d'essai est déjà le seul lien fonctionnalité↔test du
dépôt. C'est le même geste, généralisé.

pr.body:
## Why

`run_command` had exactly two controls:

1. the per-agent `command-execution` skill — the agent gets a shell, or it does not;
2. the approval gate — a human reads each command before it runs.

Neither can express *this agent runs `node` and `npx vitest`, and nothing else*. An agent whose job requires **executing** a snippet in order to check a claim (rather than reasoning about it) therefore had to be handed an unattended shell capable of anything, because an auto-approve rule turns the second control off entirely.

Milestone 0.8.10.

## What

`agents.command_allowlist` (`text[]`), as DATA on the agent row — invariant #1, no per-agent branch in the runtime.

- `NULL` = no list. Unchanged, unrestricted behaviour.
- `[]` = a decision, not an absence. Refuses every command.
- `['node', 'npx vitest']` = entries of one or more words, matched whole-token against the leading tokens of **every segment** of the command.

Enforced in `packages/tools/src/builtin/run-command.ts` before anything is resolved, and populated by the runner at the three `ToolContext` construction sites in `apps/runner/src/job/execute.ts`. Settable through the product path via `setAgentCommandAllowlistAction` (owner-only, same gate shape as `setCliRuntimeModeAction`).

### What it is not

Not a sandbox, and `command-allowlist.ts` says so in its own header: `node` can open a socket, read outside the workspace and write files. The allowlist governs **which program starts**, not what it then does. It is the third control alongside the skill and the approval gate, and it is the one that makes an auto-approved shell a defensible choice for a narrow job.

## Verified

- `packages/tools/src/builtin/command-allowlist.test.ts` — 17 tests, written before the implementation and red against a missing module. Covers `&&` / `;` / `|` / newline segments, `$()` and backtick substitution refused outright, and whole-token matching (`node` does not admit `nodemon`).
- `packages/tools/src/tests/run-command.test.ts` — 4 tool-level tests against real spawned processes. The refusal test asserts the file the refused half of the command would have written **does not exist** afterwards.
- **Mutation**: with `assertCommandAllowed(...)` disabled in `run-command.ts`, 2 of those 4 go red; restored, 16/16 pass.
- `npx vitest run packages/tools packages/db` — 91 files, 1310 passed, 1 skipped.
- `npx tsc --noEmit` on `packages/tools`, `packages/db`, `apps/runner`, `apps/web` — clean.
- `pnpm capacites:check` — the product ↔ proofs link holds (24/24 required).
- `npx eslint` on every touched file — 7 pre-existing errors in `apps/web/src/lib/actions.ts`, identical count before and after this branch; no new ones.

Migration `0108_agent_command_allowlist.sql` ships with its `_journal.json` entry and the matching column in the inline test SQL (`packages/db/src/tests/helpers.ts`) — the three places CLAUDE.md requires.

## Not in this PR

No dashboard control yet. The action exists and is the official write path; the agent editor does not surface it.

pr.body:
On 2026-09-12 an agent opened issue #68 "Publish 0.8.9" from memory. 0.8.9 had been on npm since 2026-09-09. The board carried that ghost task for four days, because nothing in the repository could contradict it. Quentin: "I can trust neither you nor my dashboard."

Three mechanisms, none of which depends on anyone remembering to be careful.

## 1. The portal reads the release state itself

`collect.mjs` asks `npm view nodal-agents version time --json` and `git` at every collection, and writes the answer into the snapshot. The board page now opens on a **Release** block: latest on npm and the day it was published, version in the repo, commits on main since the last tag.

If an OPEN card asks to publish a version npm already serves, it is **named right there** and raised as a high-severity gap. That is exactly what #68 was.

npm silent says `npm unreachable at <time>` and claims nothing: not the previous answer stripped of its date, not a green by default (invariant #4). The hourly board refresh carries the release too, because npm is not GitHub and a silent GitHub is no reason to freeze what is published.

## 2. Provenance: an agent card carries its verified facts

Rule, now in `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/skills/suivi/SKILL.md`: any issue or pull request an agent opens carries a `## Verified` section with at least one command and its output.

The portal checks it instead of trusting it. An OPEN card whose body carries the footer agents post themselves ("Generated with Claude Code", or the `Claude-Session` line) and no `## Verified` section gets a **"no verified facts"** pill on its Kanban card and is counted in the alert. The criterion is that footer and nothing else: any card carrying it is concerned, a human who pastes it included. The trade-off is deliberate, because the footer is the only verifiable signal and a style heuristic would be wrong far more often, in both directions. A card written by hand without that footer is not concerned, and that is the common case.

On the live board today this names six open cards.

## 3. `release:check` refuses to run on a live stack

`scripts/release-check.mjs` probes the web and runner ports (read from `~/.nodalai/config.json` when present) **before anything else**, and before `build-pack` empties `pack/`. It builds into `apps/web/.next`, so on a running stack it killed that stack mid-flight, and the error we then read spoke of a build and never of the stack that had just died.

```
a dev stack is running on :3000; release:check builds into apps/web/.next and
would kill it: run it from an isolated worktree or stop the stack first
```

A timeout counts as alive, not as absence: a busy server is still a server.

## Verified

Every decision is a pure function, tested red first and then verified by mutation. Ten mutations, each one named, each one turning the suite red:

| Mutation | Tests turned red |
|---|---|
| `comparerSemver` compares strings (the bug that makes 0.8.10 look older than 0.8.9) | 3 |
| npm silent still returns a value | 1 |
| `publicationsDejaFaites` ignores whether the card is open | 1 |
| "verified" as loose text counts as a section | 1 |
| the human / agent distinction dropped | 1 |
| `cartesDuTableau` stops reading issue bodies | 2 |
| one live port no longer enough to stop | 1 |
| a partial port config erases the default | 3 |
| the message no longer says what to do | 1 |
| postgres probed alongside the stack ports | 5 |

Facts this PR itself rests on:

```
$ npm view nodal-agents version
0.8.9

$ git describe --tags --abbrev=0 --match "v*"
v0.8.9

$ git rev-list --count v0.8.9..origin/main
220

$ node -p "require('./apps/cli/package.json').version"
0.8.9
```

So the repo is NOT ahead of npm today, and no open card asks to publish an already-published version. The board is telling the truth right now, and from here on it can prove it.

Gates:

```
$ pnpm --filter @nodal-agents/qa test
Test Files  6 passed (6)
     Tests  291 passed (291)

$ npx vitest run scripts/tests
Test Files  7 passed (7)
     Tests  61 passed (61)

$ node apps/qa/porte.mjs
The product <-> proofs link holds.

$ npx prettier --check "apps/qa/**/*.mjs" "scripts/**/*.mjs" CLAUDE.md .claude/skills/suivi/SKILL.md
All matched files use Prettier code style!
```

`english.test.mjs` and `nav.test.mjs` are part of the 291: the Release block and the pill are in English, and the left bar is unchanged (the block lives inside Work in flight, no new page).

Not run, and why: `pnpm typecheck` and `pnpm lint` have no surface here. Every changed file is `.mjs`, and neither `apps/qa` nor `scripts` has a `tsconfig.json`. `npx eslint scripts` reports one pre-existing error in `scripts/verify-install.mjs` that also fires on `origin/main` untouched; it is outside this change. `pnpm release:check` was not run: it builds and would have had to kill the running dev stack to prove the guard, which is the very thing the guard exists to prevent. The decision function is covered by unit tests and mutation instead.

Built and rendered from an isolated worktree; `apps/qa/data/` was restored afterwards so no local collection is committed.

## Review pass (Reviewer C, 2026-09-16)

Two MAJOR findings, both confirmed at the source, both fixed. Each is closed by a test that fails first, and each fix is verified BY MUTATION.

**1. The live-stack probe declared live stacks absent.** In `scripts/release-check.mjs`, `sonder(port)` classified every `fetch` error other than a `TimeoutError` as `vivant: false`. Two live stacks were therefore declared absent, and the guard let `release:check` build over them: a server that accepts the TCP connection then resets it or returns an unparseable response (`ECONNRESET`, malformed response), and a server bound to `::1` only when `localhost` resolves to `127.0.0.1` (refused on one family, alive on the other).

Fix: classification moved to `scripts/lib/live-stack.mjs` as pure functions (`estUnRefusDeConnexion`, `verdictDuneSonde`), so it is tested without opening a socket. `estUnRefusDeConnexion` walks `cause` and `AggregateError.errors`, because `fetch` wraps the real cause and Happy Eyeballs produces an aggregate. The network probe stays in `release-check.mjs` and now probes `127.0.0.1` and `::1` explicitly instead of `localhost`. Only a refusal proven on ALL probed families counts as absent; a reset, an invalid response, a timeout or an unknown error all count as alive, the direction that protects the stack.

Mutation verified: restoring `err?.name === 'TimeoutError'` as the verdict turns the reset / malformed-response test red.

**2. An unreadable configured port fell back silently.** In `scripts/lib/live-stack.mjs`, `portsDeLaStack` fell back to the default whenever a configured port was present but not a valid integer (`"4000"`, `0`, `-1`, `70000`, `3000.5`). The guard then probed `:3000` while the real stack served elsewhere, saw nobody, and let the build run. That is a silent smart fallback, against invariant #4.

Fix: a present-but-invalid value throws, naming the key and the value read (`ports.web = "4000" in ~/.nodalai/config.json is not a port`), and `release-check.mjs` prints that message and exits 1 before any write, so before `build-pack` empties `pack/`. An ABSENT key keeps the default: "no config" is legitimate.

Mutation verified: restoring the `Number.isInteger(v) ? v : DEFAUTS[cle]` fallback turns two tests red (string port, out-of-range / fractional port).

Gates run for this pass:

$ npx vitest run scripts/tests
Test Files  7 passed (7)
     Tests  73 passed (73)

$ npx eslint scripts/lib/live-stack.mjs scripts/release-check.mjs scripts/tests/live-stack.test.mjs
(no output)

$ npx prettier --check scripts/lib/live-stack.mjs scripts/release-check.mjs scripts/tests/live-stack.test.mjs

```

`pnpm release:check` was not run, for the same reason as above: proving this guard by running it would mean killing the dev stack it exists to protect. The probe's network layer is therefore not covered by an automated test; only the pure verdict is.

## Review pass 2 (Reviewer C, 2026-09-16)

Two MAJOR and two MINOR findings, all in `apps/qa`, all fixed. Each major is closed by a test that fails first, and every fix is verified BY MUTATION.

**MAJOR 1 - prerelease identifiers were compared as strings.** `comparerSemver` compared the whole prerelease identifier with `<`, so `1.0.0-rc.10` sorted before `1.0.0-rc.2`. An open card "Publish 1.0.0-rc.10" facing an npm serving rc.2 was named, at high severity, as asking to publish a version already on npm, while it was the newer one. That is the `0.8.10 < 0.8.9` mistake this lot exists to prevent, one level deeper.

Fix: comparison follows semver 2.0 section 11. Split on `.`, compare segment by segment, numerically when both segments are numeric, numeric before alphanumeric, and a shorter identifier that prefixes the other comes first (`rc` < `rc.1`).

Mutation verified: restoring the string comparison turns two tests red (rc.10 versus rc.2, and the card that must not be accused).

**MAJOR 2 - a "## Verified" heading quoted inside a code block counted as a section.** The heading pattern was tested against the whole body, so an agent that QUOTED the SKILL.md template inside a fenced block wrote the line without verifying anything and passed as verified. The pill that exists to catch an unverified claim was defeated by pasting the rule.

Fix: fenced segments (``` and ~~~) are removed before the heading is looked for. The scan is line by line rather than one regex, because a fence closes on the same character with at least as many marks and a block left open runs to the end of the body. A real heading before or after a block is still read. The SKILL.md template says so too, since that template is what gets pasted.

Mutation verified: dropping the stripping turns two tests red (the quoted template, and the `~~~` / unclosed-block cases).

**MINOR 1 - the docs claimed a human is never concerned.** False in the strict sense: the criterion is the agent footer, so a human who pastes "Generated with Claude Code" into their own issue body gets the pill. The rule is unchanged; the wording in `apps/qa/lib.mjs`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/skills/suivi/SKILL.md` now states it, and says why the trade-off is deliberate. The footer is the only verifiable signal, and a style heuristic would be wrong far more often, in both directions.

**MINOR 2 - two rendered pieces had no test.** The paragraph naming the open cards that ask to publish a version already on npm, and the `c.etat === 'OPEN'` condition of the "no verified facts" pill, could both be deleted with the suite staying green: the existing render tests only GREP the source of `build.mjs`, and the strings they look for are written elsewhere in the file.

`apps/qa/rendu.test.mjs` renders the portal for real, in a throwaway copy, from a snapshot built in the test, and asserts on the produced HTML. It runs in a sandbox for the same reason `collect.mjs` does: rendering in place would overwrite `apps/qa/dist` and the committed data.

Mutations verified: removing the "already on npm" paragraph turns two tests red; dropping the OPEN condition turns the closed-card test red.

## Review pass 3 (Reviewer C, 2026-09-16)

One MAJOR and five MINOR findings, all fixed. Each behaviour finding is closed by a test that fails first, and every fix is verified BY MUTATION.

**MAJOR - an unreadable config file fell back to the default ports.** `configHote` in `scripts/release-check.mjs` wrapped the read and the parse in one `catch { return null }`, so a `config.json` that EXISTS but cannot be read (invalid JSON, a UTF-8 BOM, permission denied) silently fell back to 3000/3001. The ports actually configured became invisible, the probe found nobody, and `release:check` built over the running stack while emptying `pack/`. That contradicted the loud failure already in place for an invalid port VALUE.

Fix: ABSENT and UNREADABLE are two different facts. `configHoteDepuis` in `scripts/lib/live-stack.mjs` classifies a read attempt without touching the disk. ENOENT alone means "no config" and keeps the defaults; everything else throws, naming the file and the cause. A JSON value that is not an object does not pass for a configuration either. `release-check.mjs` does the raw read and exits 1 on the message, before any write.

Mutation verified: restoring `try { JSON.parse(...) } catch { return null }` turns five tests red (EACCES, error without a code, invalid JSON, BOM, non-object JSON).

**MINOR 1 - a package that was never published was rendered as an unreachable npm.** `npm view` on a name that does not exist answers E404, and the collector threw that answer away with stderr. The portal blamed the network for a fact the registry had just established. `lectureDeNpm` now classifies three outcomes (read, never published, unreachable), `etatDeLaRelease` carries `jamaisPubliee` beside `npmInjoignable`, `collect.mjs` captures stderr where E404 lives, and the page says "Not published on npm yet" with the time of the check. Mutation verified: routing E404 back into the unreachable branch turns the classification test red.

**MINOR 2 - two edges of the fenced-block stripping.** A line indented by four spaces or a tab is an INDENTED code block in markdown, not a heading, and an indented block has no fence to strip, so pasting the template shifted right passed as verified. The heading indent is now bounded to three spaces, as markdown does, and fences too. A closing marker followed by text no longer closes a block. An unclosed fence still swallows everything after it, which is what CommonMark says and the prudent reading too; that choice is now written down and tested in both directions. Mutations verified: unbounding the heading indent turns the indented-template test red; accepting a marker with trailing text turns the closing test red.

**MINOR 3 - the "never concerned" wording.** Pass 2 corrected it in `apps/qa/lib.mjs`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/skills/suivi/SKILL.md`, but two test titles still carried the claim, and so did this PR description; all three are fixed. Verified with `grep -rn "never concerned|jamais concern" apps/qa CLAUDE.md .claude/skills/suivi/SKILL.md`, which now returns nothing.

**MINOR 4 - the npm-unreachable rendering had no render test.** `rendu.test.mjs` never rendered a snapshot with `npmInjoignable: true`. All three Release absences now render for real and are read on the HTML: npm unreachable, not published yet, and a measurement older than the check. The time assertion reads the segment rather than a formatted date, because the format depends on the timezone. Mutations verified: replacing `dateFr(r.verifieLe)` with the raw ISO string turns the unreachable test red; disabling the "not published" branch turns its test red.

**MINOR 5 - `release()` in collect.mjs had no test.** Its two decisions could be deleted with the suite staying green. `Number('')` is zero, so without the integer guard a silent git command rendered "0 commits since the tag", an assertion where there is only an absence; without the `origin/main -> HEAD` fallback, a shallow CI checkout rendered an absence where git could answer. The interpretation moves to `commitsDepuisLeTag` in lib.mjs, a pure function over the two git outputs. Mutations verified: dropping the fallback turns one test red, dropping the guard turns two red.

Test Files  7 passed (7)

$ npx vitest run scripts/tests
Test Files  7 passed (7)

$ node apps/qa/porte.mjs

$ npx prettier --check apps/qa scripts CLAUDE.md .claude/skills/suivi/SKILL.md
All matched files use Prettier code style!
```

`pnpm release:check` was not run, for the reason given above: proving that guard by running it would mean killing the dev stack it exists to protect.

## Review pass 4 (Reviewer C, 2026-09-16) - last pass

One MAJOR rejected, one MAJOR fixed, three MINOR handled. This closes the review budget for this PR.

**MAJOR, REJECTED - "no test references comparerSemver, lectureDeNpm, porteDesFaitsVerifies".** The finding is factually wrong: `apps/qa/faits.test.mjs` imports and exercises all of them. The reviewer missed the file. Counted on the branch:

```
$ grep -o "comparerSemver|lectureDeNpm|porteDesFaitsVerifies|etatDeLaRelease|publicationsDejaFaites|sansFaitsVerifies|ecritParUnAgent|commitsDepuisLeTag" apps/qa/faits.test.mjs | wc -l
103
```

No change made.

**MAJOR - an empty "## Verified" heading proved nothing.** The rule says "at least one command and its output", but the check only looked for the heading. A bare `## Verified`, or one followed by prose, earned a clean bill: the pill could be bought with five characters, which emptied the rule of its purpose.

A section now has to carry CODE before the next heading of level <= its own: an inline span, a fenced block, or a four-space indented block. A sub-heading stays inside the section; a proof filed after the next same-level heading does not count for it.

One deliberate departure from the finding as written, and it matters. The finding asked for a fenced or indented block ONLY. But the template in `.claude/skills/suivi/SKILL.md` writes its proofs as inline spans (`npm view nodal-agents version` -> 0.8.9), so requiring a block would have flagged every correctly filled card, including the ones this rule was written for. Inline code is therefore accepted, and the rule text in `apps/qa/lib.mjs`, `CLAUDE.md` and `SKILL.md` now spells out the three accepted forms.

Mutation verified: returning true on the heading alone turns three tests red (empty heading, prose-only section, proof filed after the next heading).

**MINOR 1 - any 404 in stderr counted as "never published".** A corporate proxy answering 404 for an unrelated reason writes that number too, so an access failure would have been rendered as "this package does not exist". Only npm's own code line counts now. The real output of `npm view <missing> --json` on npm 11 is `npm error code E404` followed by `npm error 404 Not Found - GET ...`; older npm writes `npm ERR! code E404`. Both forms are matched, plus `error.code === 'E404'` in the JSON npm puts on stdout, and nothing else. Mutation verified: widening the test back to any 404 anywhere turns the proxy test red.

**MINOR 2 - a 307 towards a closed address made the probe declare the stack absent.** `fetch` follows redirects by default, so the ECONNREFUSED came from the SECOND request, and a stack that had just answered was read as a proven refusal. `redirect: 'manual'` fixes it: a 3xx is a response.

The probe also moved out of `release-check.mjs` into `scripts/lib/sonde.mjs`, and that is the substance of the change beyond the one option. `release-check.mjs` runs the whole release check on import, so nothing in it could ever be tested, and this option is exactly the kind of thing no source reading proves. The probe now answers real servers in `scripts/tests/sonde.test.mjs`: 200, 500, a 307 to a dead port, a connection accepted then destroyed, a dead port, and one address family refusing while the other serves. The verdict stays pure in `live-stack.mjs`. Mutation verified: dropping `redirect: 'manual'` turns the 307 test red.
